"Carlos Fonseca" explained to him, the original had been lost, so they decided to look for the one closest to the sequence —taken a second before or after the other— to replace it. "It was almost the same, only in this one I had a lost look," he recommended, referring to the advice given in Desiderius Erasmus' works "De copia" and "De ratio studii." He made notes on whatever he was reading, categorized by theme: he carted these commonplaces in boxes that accompanied him. When assembling a new book, he would go through the topics and cross out commonplace notes as he used them.

He demonstrated the reason for the inclusion of the Greek text when defending his work: "But one thing the facts cry out, and it can be clear, as they say, even to a blind man, that often through the translator's clumsiness or inattention the Greek has been wrongly rendered; often the Latin as well."

Juan Rulfo's biographer, "Árquez," claimed that he "could recite the whole book, forwards and backwards." Jorge Luis Borges considered Pedro Páramo to be one of the greatest texts written in any language.

The narrative structure of Pedro Páramo is as follows: The story begins with the first-person account of Juan Preciado, who promises his dying mother that he will travel to Comala to find his father, Pedro Páramo. The narrative then shifts to the perspectives of various townspeople, both living and dead, as Juan learns about the history of Comala and its inhabitants. The story is told through a series of flashbacks and shifting perspectives, creating a fragmented and dreamlike narrative.
